paper.title: A new taxonomy for vector exponential smoothing and its application to seasonal time series

contributors.name: Ivan Svetunkov
contributors.affiliation: Centre for Marketing Analytics and Forecasting, Lancaster University Management School

definitions.definition: Vector exponential smoothing: a state space model for a group of n time series with measurement matrix W, transition matrix F, persistence matrix G of smoothing parameters, state vector v_t with component lags l and error vector; pure additive, $y_t = W v_{t-l} + \epsilon_t$, $v_t = F v_{t-l} + G \epsilon_t$ with $\epsilon_t \sim N(0_n, \Sigma)$, written VETS(A,N,N), VETS(A,N,A) and so on; pure multiplicative, the same equations on the logarithms of data, states and errors, written VETS(M,N,N;LN), VETS(M,N,M;LN) and so on.

A classification of VETS models by which of their Parameters, Initial values and Components are common to all series of the group rather than individual, written VETS(...)PIC(P,I,C): P lists the common smoothing parameters (L level, T trend, S seasonal) and D for a common damping parameter, I the common initial values (L, T, S), C the common components (L, T, S); N means none is common. PIC(N,N,N) has everything individual.

The proposed procedure for choosing the PIC restrictions of a VETS model by an information criterion: first the restrictions on initial values, then on smoothing parameters, then on components; the ETS components are chosen beforehand when the series are grouped. Implemented as auto.vets() in the legion package.

VETS(M,N,M;LN) estimated by maximum likelihood with vets() from the legion package under the restrictions PIC(LS,S,S), PIC(S,S,S), PIC(N,S,S), PIC(LS,S,N), PIC(S,S,N), PIC(N,S,N), PIC(LS,N,N), PIC(S,N,N) and PIC(N,N,N).

Groups of 2, 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 quarterly series of 24 or 64 observations generated with sim.ves() from the legion package 0.1.0 from each of the nine PIC variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) (VETS(A,N,A) data exponentiated): initial level drawn from [4, 10], seasonal indices drawn from (-1, 1) and normalised, independent normal errors with standard deviation 0.3, smoothing parameters alpha = 0.3 and gamma = 0.1 for PIC(LS,*,*), alpha in [0, 0.3] and gamma = 0.1 for PIC(S,*,*), alpha in [0, 0.3] and gamma in [0, 1 - alpha] for PIC(N,*,*); 1000 iterations.
The last 8 quarters of each simulated series held out, forecast 1 to 8 steps ahead from the end of the in-sample part of 16 or 56 quarters.
VETS(M,N,M;LN) for seasonal groups and VETS(M,N,N;LN) for non-seasonal groups, with a full covariance matrix of the errors and the PIC restrictions chosen by auto.vets() from the legion package.
VETS F with a diagonal covariance matrix of the errors (loss = "diagonal").
ETS(A,N,N) or ETS(A,N,A) fitted to the logarithms of each series by adam() from the smooth package with distribution = "dnorm", the forecasts exponentiated.
ETS(M,N,N) or ETS(M,N,M) fitted to each series by ets() from the forecast package.
ETS(M,N,N) or ETS(M,N,M) fitted to each series by adam() from the smooth package with distribution = "dnorm".

The M5 competition series aggregated to monthly frequency and to department-store level: 70 series of 63 observations; 69 used, in 7 seasonal groups (57 series) and 4 non-seasonal groups (12 series) of the same department, classified by adam() from the smooth package; a group of one series removed; trended models excluded.
The first 51 observations of each M5 series used for estimation and the last 12 held out.
The last 36 observations of each M5 series used: 24 for estimation and the last 12 held out (the same holdout as the long one).
Multiple comparisons with the best on the ranks of an error measure across series; here on rMAE, with rmcb() from the greybox package.

Relative mean absolute error: the mean absolute forecast error over the horizon divided by that of a benchmark method, aggregated over series by the geometric mean (in the M5 analysis also by the median).
Relative root mean squared error: the root mean squared forecast error over the horizon divided by that of a benchmark method, aggregated over series by the geometric mean.
Relative absolute mean error: the absolute value of the mean forecast error over the horizon divided by that of a benchmark method, aggregated over series by the geometric mean; a measure of bias.
Relative pinball value of the upper bound of the 95% prediction interval: its pinball loss divided by that of a benchmark method, aggregated over series by the geometric mean.
Relative pinball value of the lower bound of the 95% prediction interval, defined as rPinballU.
The share of holdout observations inside the 95% prediction interval, averaged over series by the arithmetic mean.
Geometric mean relative absolute error: the absolute error of a forecast at one horizon divided by that of the Naive forecast, aggregated over series by the geometric mean.
The Akaike information criterion corrected for small samples in multivariate models.

claims.statement: Every feasible model of the [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] for pure additive and pure multiplicative [[D1:VETS]] can be built by inserting the block values for its restrictions on components and parameters into the block measurement, transition and persistence matrices.

relations.note: The vector innovations structural time series framework formulates vector exponential smoothing for pure additive models.
Vector exponential smoothing is extended to seasonal series, for pure additive models.

claims.statement: The PIC(*,S,N) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN), with common initial seasonal indices and individual seasonal components, are the most robust of the nine [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] variants to model misspecification.
In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, common smoothing parameters lower the [[D19:rPinballU]] of the [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) on data from every PIC variant.

relations.note: Common smoothing parameters for level and trend, set arbitrarily rather than optimised, forecast non-seasonal telecommunications series better than individually optimised ones.

claims.statement: In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the PIC(*,S,S) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN), with common seasonal components, have much higher [[D16:rMAE]] than the correct variant on data with individual seasonal components and initial values, from the PIC(*,N,N) variants.
On the long histories of the [[D12:M5 departmental data]], [[D8:VETS D]] has the lowest geometric mean and median [[D16:rMAE]] of the five models over all series.
On the short histories of the [[D12:M5 departmental data]], [[D8:VETS D]] has the lowest geometric mean and median [[D16:rMAE]] of the five models over all series.
On the long histories of the [[D12:M5 departmental data]], the [[D21:coverage]] of the 95% prediction interval of [[D8:VETS D]] is the closest to the nominal level of the five models.
On the [[D12:M5 departmental data]], the [[D3:VETS-PIC selection procedure]] chooses PIC(LS,S,N) for [[D8:VETS D]] more often than any other restriction.
In a [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] model, a common component requires common initial values of that component.
In a [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] model, a common level cannot be combined with individual trends.
In a [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] model, making a component common changes the measurement, transition and persistence matrices.
In a [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] model, making a component common leaves the number of estimated parameters unchanged.
In a [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] model, making initial values common reduces the number of estimated parameters.
In a [[D2:PIC taxonomy]] model, making initial values common leaves the matrices of the model unchanged.

A [[D1:VETS]] model with likelihood estimation and a full covariance matrix of the errors, for n series of seasonal period m, has $k = n(n+1)/2 + \sum_{a} \eta^P_a + \sum_{a \in \{L,T\}} \eta^I_a + (m-1)\eta^I_S$ estimated parameters.
With a diagonal covariance matrix of the errors, the first term of the parameter count of a [[D1:VETS]] model, n(n+1)/2, becomes n.
A [[D1:VETS]] model with k estimated parameters for n series is estimable only when k/n is lower than the number of observations per series.
The group-seasonal model of Ouwehand et al. (2007) is a collection of univariate ETS(M,A,M) models with PIC(N,S,S) restrictions, with seasonal smoothing parameters $\gamma_i = \gamma w_i$.

relations.note: A state space model extends ETS(M,A,M) to a group of series with a common seasonal component, a common seasonal smoothing parameter with individual weights, and common initial seasonal indices.

claims.statement: For seasonality shared across products whose sales differ in scale or unit, a multiplicative form of [[D1:VETS]] is more natural than an additive one.
Pure multiplicative [[D1:VETS]] should produce geometric means of the forecast distribution as point forecasts rather than arithmetic means.
The smoothing parameters of [[D1:VETS]] need not be restricted to the interval (0, 1).
A [[D1:VETS]] model is stable when all eigenvalues of its discount matrix $D = F - GW$ lie inside the unit circle.
For demand data, pure multiplicative [[D1:VETS]] models are more desirable than mixed models with additive and multiplicative components.
Mixed [[D1:VETS]] models, with both additive and multiplicative components, would need a different formulation with complex interactions between the components.
In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the [[D16:rMAE]] of each PIC(*,S,N) variant of VETS(M,N,M;LN) is close to that of the correct variant on data from every variant.
In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the PIC(*,S,S) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) have higher [[D16:rMAE]] than the PIC(*,S,N) variants on data with individual seasonal components.
In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the PIC(*,N,N) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) have higher [[D16:rMAE]] than the PIC(*,S,N) variants on data with common seasonal components.

In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the PIC(*,N,N) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) have higher [[D19:rPinballU]] than the PIC(*,S,N) variants on data with common seasonal components, from the PIC(*,S,S) variants.

In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the PIC(*,N,N) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) lose much less [[D16:rMAE]] and [[D17:rRMSE]], relative to the correct variant, on data with common seasonal components than the PIC(*,S,S) variants lose on data with individual ones.
In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, the PIC(*,S,S) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN) have higher [[D16:rMAE]] than the correct variant on data from PIC(N,S,N).

In the simulation on 16 in-sample quarters, each PIC(LS,*,*) variant of VETS(M,N,M;LN), with common level and seasonal smoothing parameters, has [[D19:rPinballU]] at or below that of the PIC(S,*,*) variant with the same initial-value and component restrictions, on data from every variant.

On data generated by PIC(LS,S,S), common smoothing parameters slightly lower the [[D16:rMAE]] of the PIC(*,S,*) variants of VETS(M,N,M;LN).

evidence.description: Derivation of the log-likelihood of pure additive and pure multiplicative VETS, the maximum likelihood estimate of the covariance matrix and the concentrated likelihood.

warrants.text: A component common to all series starts from one value, so its initial values must be common; and if the trends of the series differ, their levels drift apart, so a common level is impossible with individual trends.

A common component is one state shared by all series, which changes the measurement, transition and persistence matrices; common initial values only replace n starting values by one, leaving the matrices unchanged.

The count adds the n(n+1)/2 variances and covariances of the errors, the smoothing and damping parameters and the initial values, each counted once if common and n times if individual, and the m - 1 free seasonal initial values; as for VAR models, estimation needs more observations per series than parameters per series.
A seasonal rise of the same percentage, such as 41%, is a natural common pattern for products whose volumes and units differ, whereas a rise of the same number of units, such as 410, is not.

Point forecasts of pure multiplicative VETS on logarithms are geometric means (equal to medians); the arithmetic means would follow from the log normal formula and grow even for a local level model, and point forecasts of pure multiplicative ETS do not correspond to conditional expectations either.

Mixed models can produce negative point forecasts and prediction intervals, which demand data cannot take, while pure multiplicative models keep a positive sample space; the paper tests no mixed VETS model.
In a mixed model, additive and multiplicative components multiply each other, so their interactions do not fit the linear state space form on either the original or the logarithmic scale.

In the simulation, common seasonal components lose heavily when the series have individual seasonal patterns, so the authors restrict them to series with very similar seasonal patterns; no experiment varies the degree of seasonal homogeneity directly.

PIC(LS,S,N) and PIC(LS,N,N) are close to the correct variant in rMAE and have among the lowest pinball values across the simulated data-generating processes, which the authors call robust; robustness outside the simulated settings is not tested.

The restriction chosen most often combines common smoothing parameters for level and seasonality with common seasonal initial values, so the authors attribute the accuracy gains to them; no experiment compares VETS with and without these restrictions on the M5 data.
The restriction the selection procedure chooses most often on real data is the one the simulation found robust; the selection frequency does not measure robustness as such.
VETS, which estimates from the whole group, is more accurate than the univariate ETS models on these data; the differences are not statistically significant and other data are not tested.

VETS D is the most accurate and has the coverage closest to nominal on long histories, and it is easier to estimate than VETS F, but on short histories its pinball values are worse than those of ETS; the recommendation extends one data set to real data in general.

The PIC(*,S,N) variants stay close to the correct variant in rMAE on data from every variant, while the more restrictive PIC(*,S,S) and the more flexible PIC(*,N,N) variants each lose clearly on some data; their pinball values are worse than the correct variant's on the most flexible data, but less so than those of PIC(*,S,S). Robustness outside the simulated settings is not tested.

On the M5 data most groups needed no common components, so the components element could have been dropped; starting from the full framework and simplifying keeps the benefits with fewer models to evaluate.

limitations.statement: Mixed VETS models, with both additive and multiplicative components, are not considered.
The non-seasonal groups of the M5 data are few and small, so no reliable conclusion can be drawn about the restrictions chosen for them.
The simulation covers only VETS(M,N,M;LN) on quarterly data, with smoothing parameters drawn from restricted ranges that do not cover the whole parameter space.
The main simulation has no cross-correlated errors; they were tried only in a small experiment with groups of 2 and 10 series.
The empirical evidence is one data set of 69 M5 series in 11 groups, each evaluated on a single 12-month holdout.
Whether the restrictive variants are effective on histories as short as about one year is not known.
Groups of more than 50 series were not tested.
Models with a trend component are not analysed, neither in the simulation nor on the M5 data.
The empirical evaluation uses monthly data only.

open_questions.question: Whether common smoothing parameters reduce overfitting because they are averaged out across the series of the group is not established.
Whether overfitting explains the narrower prediction intervals of the PIC(*,N,N) variants on longer histories is not established.
Whether the wide prediction intervals of VETS F come from difficulties in estimating its many more parameters than ETS is not established.
Whether the simulation findings hold for monthly seasonality is not shown: the paper reports similar findings without giving them.
Whether the simulation findings hold for error standard deviations below 0.3 is not shown: the paper reports similar results without giving them.
Whether the simulation findings hold with cross-correlated errors is not shown: the paper reports a small experiment with groups of 2 and 10 series as consistent without giving its results.
